newsitem.title: INDIA: India polls likely outcome of Deve Gowda's fall.
newsitem.headline: India polls likely outcome of Deve Gowda's fall.

text.p: Early elections loomed in India on Saturday after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda lost a vote of confidence in parliament, political parties said.
"I hope sooner than later Deve Gowda will come back as prime minister," Somnath Chatterjee a communist leader of the defeated United Front alliance told Reuters after the vote.
"There is an attempt by some people in the United Front to form a government, but there is no arithmetic to support that move which we oppose. There is no alternative to polls."

He was apparently referring to a reported move by Finance Minister P.Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress to hold talks with the Congress party which triggered the government's fall by withdrawing its crucial support on March 30.
Deve Gowda's Janata Dal with some 32 deputies and the Left Front partners controlling about 50 members were against a new coalition with the Congress, saying it was an unreliable ally.
The Congress has 140 deputies against 193 of the BJP and the United Front's 178.
Criticism of the Congress move was voiced by some of its own deputies.
"I for one obeyed the whip and voted against my conscience," said former Congress chief minister A.R. Antulay after he followed the party's mandate to vote out the government.
"It is true that I did pledge my support to Deve Gowda when he became prime minister in June. Today I voted as a disciplined soldier of the party but not without regret."
Antulay was joined by another former chief minister of Mahrashtra, Sharad Pawar, who said the Congress was aware that polls could be unavoidable.
"We are prepared for any eventuality," Pawar told reporters. he said. "The first chapter is over. We have to find out what the second part holds for us."
Much of the 12-hour debate on Deve Gowda's motion of confidence centred on Pawar's remark that the Congress decision to withdraw support had come to him as a bolt from the blue.
India's main opposition group, the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said it would press for polls if it was unable to form its own government.

"We will stake a claim to form the government only if we have the required majority," BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj told Reuters. "Dissolution of the house will become inevitable if we can't get a majority."
President Shankar Dayal Sharma may call another candidate to succeed Deve Gowda but only if he is satisifed that the claimant has a reasonable support in parliament, BJP deputies said.
Communist Home Minister Inderjit Gupta said he saw little possibility of anyone succeeding to form a government with a clear majority.
Asked if that meant mid-term polls, he said: "That's very likely."

Among the United Front leaders whose names were mentioned by some deputies as those locked in an effort to form a government with Congress support were Chidambaram, his party boss G.K. Moopanar, Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav and Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan.
But former Congress minister Santosh Mohan Deb said his party had not given up its own chances of seeking to head a coalition.
"The Congress can also try to lead a coalition," he said.
That prospect appeared unrealistic, other Congress leaders said.
"There is a major difference between hope and possibility," said former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"Let's see what happens now," said a dejected-looking Rao, who was among the Congress leaders who reluctantly voted against Deve Gowda on Friday.
